title: Foods that lower cholesterol: a guide to better meal swaps
summary: 30 example meals, four calculated swaps, and what diet trials found about LDL.
body_markdown:
Diet can lower your cholesterol in a counterintuitive way. The most important nutrients for lowering LDL aren’t dietary cholesterol, but fiber (get more) and saturated fat (get less).


We’ll compare how much diets and individual foods lower LDL, then plot meals on a fiber–saturated-fat grid to find useful swaps.


## How much can diet lower LDL cholesterol?


In a[six-month trial of 345 adults](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21862744/) , the Portfolio diet (nuts, soy protein, viscous fiber, and plant sterols) lowered LDL by 13.1–13.8% from baseline, compared with 3.0% for a low-saturated-fat comparison diet. A 13% reduction from LDL 160 mg/dL is about 21 mg/dL, though individual results vary. If you need a larger reduction to reach your goal, diet can work alongside[LDL-lowering medications](https://www.empirical.health/blog/ldl-cholesterol-lowering-medications/) .


## What foods lower LDL cholesterol?


A[2021 review of 108 systematic reviews](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.numecd.2020.12.032) compared foods by LDL effect and evidence strength, covering research through June 2019. The strongest evidence supports replacing saturated fats with unsaturated oils, eating soluble-fiber foods, and using foods with added plant sterols or stanols.


*Figure 3 from[Schoeneck and Iggman, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.numecd.2020.12.032) , reproduced under[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) ; cropped from the original page. Foods below the line lower LDL; foods above it raise LDL. Larger circles indicate high-certainty evidence; smaller circles indicate moderate certainty. Positions illustrate relative effects, not precise estimates.*


In the table below, small means under about 8 mg/dL, moderate means about 8–15 mg/dL, and large means over about 15 mg/dL. Doses and comparison foods differ across studies.


Food or change Reported LDL reduction Evidence certainty A way to use it


Unsaturated oils replacing saturated fats Moderate to large High Replace butter with canola or olive oil


Oats, barley, psyllium Moderate High Choose oats or barley for soluble fiber


Foods with added plant sterols or stanols Moderate High Look for fortified foods; ordinary plant foods aren’t equivalent doses


Whole flaxseed, soy protein, tomatoes Small to moderate High Add ground flaxseed to oats, or use tofu and tomatoes in a meal


Almonds Small High Use as a snack or topping


Avocado Moderate to large Moderate Use in a sandwich or on toast


Beans, lentils, hazelnuts Small to moderate Moderate Replace some meat with beans or lentils


Walnuts, whole grains Small Moderate Add walnuts to breakfast or choose whole-grain bread


You can’t add these reductions together. Portions and replacement foods differ; the Portfolio trial above tested a combination directly.


### What else affects cholesterol?


Fiber and saturated fat don’t capture every dietary effect. Unfiltered coffee can raise LDL, while filtered coffee had no effect in this review; see[which brewing methods affect cholesterol](https://www.empirical.health/blog/does-coffee-raise-cholesterol/) .


Food structure matters, too. In a[trial of 92 people](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28251937/) , LDL was 3.3% lower with a cheese-rich diet than a butter-rich diet containing the same saturated fat. It was still higher than with diets rich in unsaturated fat. Fish had no clear LDL effect in the review, which doesn’t mean it has no other health benefits.

The central axes divide the examples, not clinical cutoffs. Scroll sideways on small screens. Ingredient weights and nutrient calculations are available below.*


Quadrant Example meal What could you change?


More fiber, less saturated fat Lentil, rice and tomato bowl Use it as a starting point for other bean or lentil meals


Less fiber, less saturated fat Chicken and rice bowl Replace some rice with beans


More fiber, more saturated fat Whole-wheat grilled cheese with beans Keep the beans; reduce the cheese and replace butter with oil


Less fiber, more saturated fat Cheeseburger Replace some beef with beans and use whole-grain bread


The grid shows total fiber; the strongest LDL evidence is for soluble fiber. Even soluble fibers differ: an[oat-cereal trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20660224/) found that beta-glucan’s molecular weight affected LDL lowering. The grid doesn’t predict a meal’s LDL effect or overall healthfulness.


### What meal swaps help you move up and left?


We calculated four recipe swaps using USDA data. The table shows nutrients per serving.


Change Calories, before → after Fiber Saturated fat Protein Source


Butter → olive oil on whole-wheat toast 273 → 273 4.8 → 4.8 g 5.7 → 1.7 g 10 → 10 g USDA SR Legacy


Half the beef → beans in a rice bowl 463 → 465 1.8 → 9.2 g 6.0 → 3.2 g 31 → 27 g USDA SR Legacy


White → whole-wheat bread in a chicken sandwich 354 → 343 2.8 → 5.4 g 1.4 → 1.4 g 32 → 35 g USDA SR Legacy


Whole-milk → nonfat yogurt in an oat bowl 301 → 292 6.0 → 6.0 g 4.0 → 0.7 g 12 → 16 g USDA SR Legacy


In the rice bowl, we replaced 100 grams of cooked beef with 50 grams of beef and 100 grams of cooked kidney beans, keeping the rice and tomato unchanged.


Choose the swap that improves your meal: whole-grain bread adds fiber; replacing butter with oil lowers saturated fat.


Brand and portion size affect the numbers. Our[ingredient weights](https://www.empirical.health/data/cholesterol-food-guide/recipe-ingredients.csv) ,[USDA nutrient records](https://www.empirical.health/data/cholesterol-food-guide/usda-ingredients-per-100g.csv) , and[recipe totals](https://www.empirical.health/data/cholesterol-food-guide/recipe-totals.csv) are available to check or adapt.


### How do you know whether the changes are working?


Log your meals in[Empirical Health](https://www.empirical.health/blog/nutrition-calculator-ai/) and agree on a follow-up blood test with your clinician. Record medication changes too, so you can interpret whether your diet and treatment are bringing LDL toward your goal.


How we calculated the meals and swaps


The 30 example meals and four recipe pairs use the USDA SR Legacy dataset. They are illustrative recipes, not user meal logs or meals tested in a clinical trial.


We summed each ingredient’s nutrients per 100 grams multiplied by its edible weight. Rice, pasta, meat, beans, lentils, and vegetables use the preparation states listed in the downloadable ingredient records. Oats use dry weight; tofu uses a firm raw-tofu record. Coconut milk uses the USDA raw, full-fat coconut-milk record (expressed from grated coconut and water), which differs from canned products and coconut beverages. Ground beef uses the cooked, broiled 85% lean record. The cheeseburger uses a generic commercial white-bread record for its bread portion. We added no unlisted cooking fat. Actual brands and preparation will differ.


The meal cards and tables show nutrients per actual serving. Rounding occurs after calculation. The photos are AI-generated illustrations of the recipes, not photographs of weighed portions or user meals. Nutrient calculations do not establish a clinical LDL response.


The table lists portions for 15 examples; downloads below cover all 30. Rice, meat, lentils, and beans are weighed cooked; oats are weighed dry.
